raw_case_text:
A 16-year-old, previously healthy teen presented to emergency department with complaints of high-grade intermittent fever for a week followed by severe periumbilical pain with multiple episodes of loose stools, vomiting, and jaundice for 3 days. He did not have history of drug or alcohol abuse and never received blood transfusions in the past. He did not have history of recent travel or trauma.
On examination, he looked ill and toxic but was conscious and well oriented. He was icteric and mildly dehydrated although hemodynamically stable. Temperature was recorded to be 101 F. He was in mild respiratory distress with a respiratory rate of 32/min and SpO2 of 98% on O2 at 4 litres per minute via face mask. Abdominal examination revealed tenderness with guarding over the periumbilical region and hepatosplenomegaly. Rest of the systemic examination was unremarkable. The investigations revealed a deranged LFT with direct hyperbilirubinemia (total 4.6 mg/dl, direct 2.3 mg/dl) and elevated enzymes (ALP 273 mu/l, AST 214 mu/l, ALT 123 mu/l, and G-GT 294 mu/l). The pancreatic enzymes were also elevated (Amylase-548 mu/l and Lipase-415 mu/l), whereas renal function tests and hemogram were both normal.
Plain abdominal radiographs showed colon cut-off and sentinel loop signs as shown in Figures 1 and 2. Ultrasound abdomen revealed hyperechoic pancreas, distended gall bladder, and splenomegaly. Further evaluation with an abdominal contrast enhanced computed tomography showed bulky pancreatic tail and body with mild soft tissue stranding in the peripancreatic fat, distended gall bladder with minimal pericholecystic fluid, and minimal ascites with hepatosplenomegaly. There was also bilateral minimal pleural effusion with subsegmental atelectasis of posterobasal segment of both lower lung lobes. Features favored acute interstitial pancreatitis: Modified Computed Tomography Severity Index (CTSI) score of 4 as shown in Figures 3-9.
Aided by Revised Atlanta Classification of AP 2012, a clinicoradiological diagnosis of interstitial edematous pancreatitis without pancreatic necrosis was made. Severity and mortality assessment done using Ranson's criteria at admission and within 48 hours predicted an associated mortality of 0-3%.
He was admitted to the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit (PICU), with a diagnosis of AP with impending septic shock and jaundice. Based on clinical findings, infective etiology was considered, and broad-spectrum antibiotics were initiated after sending blood culture and serological tests. He was kept nil by mouth, given intravenous fluid resuscitation, analgesics, and antipyretics.
After 4 days of intensive monitoring and supportive care, his fever and pain subsided. He could be gradually started on oral fluids and then on to fat-free diet. On day 6, he was stable to be transferred to the general ward, where he received a complete course of antibiotics for ten days and made an uneventful recovery.
LFT, serum proteins, and pancreatic enzymes were followed up till discharge and at 2 months, wherein gradual normalization in all was noted as shown in Figures 10-13.
Laboratory findings during hospitalization and at 2 months follow-up:
The serological tests for hepatitis B, C, leptospira, malaria antigen, and dengue were all reported negative, while the Widal test yielded positive for S. typhi "O" (1 : 320) and "H" (1 : 320). Based upon growth of "Salmonella enterica serovar typhi" on the blood culture 72 hours later, a final complete diagnosis of AP and AH secondary to Salmonella typhi infection was made.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 16-year-old male presented with high-grade intermittent fever for 1 week followed by severe periumbilical pain, loose stools, vomiting, and jaundice for 3 days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: High-grade intermittent fever started 1 week prior to presentation. Four days later, he developed severe periumbilical pain, multiple episodes of loose stools, vomiting, and jaundice over the preceding 3 days.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy. Denied alcohol or drug abuse, blood transfusions, recent travel, or trauma.
subjective.review_of_systems: Loose stools, vomiting, jaundice, mild shortness of breath.

objective.physical_examination: Ill and toxic-looking but conscious and oriented; icteric and mildly dehydrated; hemodynamically stable. Temperature: 101 °F. Mild respiratory distress with respiratory rate 32/min, SpO2 98% on 4 L/min oxygen via face mask. Abdomen: tenderness and guarding over the periumbilical region; hepatosplenomegaly. Rest of systemic examination unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Liver function tests: total bilirubin 4.6 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 2.3 mg/dL, ALP 273 mU/L, AST 214 mU/L, ALT 123 mU/L, GGT 294 mU/L. Pancreatic enzymes: amylase 548 mU/L, lipase 415 mU/L. Renal function tests and hemogram: normal. Plain abdominal radiographs: colon cut-off and sentinel loop signs. Abdominal ultrasound: hyperechoic pancreas, distended gallbladder, splenomegaly. Serology: hepatitis B, hepatitis C, leptospira, malaria antigen, and dengue tests all negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT: bulky pancreatic tail and body with mild soft tissue stranding in peripancreatic fat, distended gallbladder with minimal pericholecystic fluid, minimal ascites, hepatosplenomegaly, and bilateral minimal pleural effusion with subsegmental atelectasis of posterobasal segments of lower lung lobes; Modified Computed Tomography Severity Index (CTSI) score of 4, consistent with interstitial edematous pancreatitis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Acute interstitial edematous pancreatitis and acute hepatitis secondary to Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi infection (typhoid fever), complicated by impending septic shock. Blood cultures grew Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi at 72 hours, and Widal test was positive for S. typhi O (1:320) and H (1:320). Managed in the PICU: kept NPO, received IV fluid resuscitation, analgesics, antipyretics, and broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics. Fever and abdominal pain resolved after 4 days; oral fluids and fat-free diet were initiated. Transferred to the general ward on day 6 and completed a 10-day antibiotic course with uneventful recovery. Follow-up LFTs, serum proteins, and pancreatic enzymes gradually normalized and were completely normal at 2-month follow-up.
